facts.statement: The genus Aepyornis was described by I. Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire in 1851.
facts.quote: authority: I. Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire, 1851

facts.statement: The genus Aepyornis became extinct around 1000 AD.
facts.quote: extinct: 1000 AD

facts.statement: Aepyornis was an extinct genus of elephant birds that lived only on Madagascar.
facts.quote: Aepyornis is an extinct genus of elephant bird formerly endemic to Madagascar.

facts.statement: The closest living relative of Aepyornis is the New Zealand kiwi.
facts.quote: Its closest living relative is the New Zealand kiwi.

facts.statement: DNA comparisons suggest elephant birds diverged from New Zealand kiwis over 50 million years ago.
facts.quote: More recently, it has been deduced from DNA sequence comparisons that the closest living relatives of elephant birds are the New Zealand kiwis, from which they were estimated to have diverged over 50 million years ago.

facts.statement: Aepyornis was a ratite that could not fly and lacked a keel on its breast bone.
facts.quote: Like the cassowaries, ostriches, rheas, emu and kiwis, the elephant birds were ratites; they could not fly, and their breast bones had no keel.

facts.statement: A. maximus weighed between 275 and 1000 kg and reached a height of 3 meters.
facts.quote: The species of Aepyornis are amongst the largest birds, with weights of 235 kg estimated for A. hildebrandti and 275-1000 kg for A. maximus, making it one of the largest, if not the largest bird to have ever lived, with the latter reaching 3 m in height.

facts.statement: Both species had small heads with straight, thick conical beaks, though the beak was proportionally larger in A. hildebrandti.
facts.quote: The head bore a straight, thick conical beak, which was proportionally larger in A. hildebrandti than in A. maximus, though the heads in both birds were small relative to body size.

facts.statement: The neck of Aepyornis was proportionally long, containing 16 to 17 cervical vertebrae.
facts.quote: The neck was proportionally long, with 16-17 cervical vertebrae.

facts.statement: The wings of Aepyornis were vestigial.
facts.quote: The wings were vestigial.

facts.statement: The pelvic bones of Aepyornis were heavily fused, making their individual boundaries difficult to discern.
facts.quote: The pelvic bones (vertebrae, ilium and pubis) were heavily fused to each other, so much so that their boundaries are difficult to discern.

facts.statement: The hindlimbs were proportionally long and robust, with a particularly short and thick femur.
facts.quote: The hindlimb was proportionally long, with its bones being robust, with the femur in particular being very short and thick.

facts.statement: The terminal toe bones of Aepyornis were broad and not hooked.
facts.quote: The terminal toe bones (phalanges) of the foot are broad and not hooked.

facts.statement: Brain endocasts show that Aepyornis had greatly reduced optic lobes, consistent with a nocturnal lifestyle.
facts.quote: Examination of brain endocasts has shown that both A. maximus and A. hildebrandti had greatly reduced optic lobes, similar to those of their closest living relatives, the kiwis, and consistent with a similar nocturnal lifestyle.

facts.statement: Larger olfactory bulbs in A. maximus suggest it occupied forested habitats, while A. hildebrandti likely occupied open habitats.
facts.quote: A. maximus had relatively larger olfactory bulbs than A. hildebrandti, suggesting that the former occupied forested habitats where the sense of smell is more useful while the latter occupied open habitats.

facts.statement: A 2022 isotope study suggested A. hildebrandti was a mixed feeder with a large grazing component, while A. maximus was probably a browser.
facts.quote: A 2022 isotope analysis study suggested that individuals of Aepyornis hildebrandti from central Madagascar were mixed feeders that had a large (~48%) grazing component to its diet, similar to that of the living Rhea americana, while A. maximus was probably a browser.

facts.statement: Aepyornis eggs are the largest known for any amniote, with volumes of 5.6 to 13 litres.
facts.quote: The eggs of Aepyornis are the largest known for any amniote, and have a volume of around 5.6–13 litres, and a length of approximately 26–40 cm and a width of 19–25 cm.

facts.statement: An Aepyornis egg has about 160 times the volume of a chicken egg.
facts.quote: The egg is about 160 times greater volume than a chicken egg.

facts.statement: An intact embryonic skeleton of Aepyornis was found in an egg that was 80-90% of the way through incubation.
facts.quote: An embryonic skeleton of Aepyornis is known from an intact egg, around 80-90% of the way through incubation before it died.

facts.statement: Possible remnants of medullary bone used for egg calcium have been found in the femurs of A. maximus.
facts.quote: The large size of elephant bird eggs means that they would have required substantial amounts of calcium, which is usually taken from a reservoir in the medullary bone in the femurs of female birds. Possible remnants of this tissue have been described from the femurs of A. maximus.

facts.statement: Later DNA studies suggest Vorombe titan is indistinguishable from A. maximus and likely represents large females of that species.
facts.quote: However, later DNA studies found that Vorombe titan was indistinguishable from A. maximus, and probably represented large females of the species.

facts.statement: DNA from Aepyornis eggs was successfully extracted and published in 2010.
facts.quote: After many years of failed attempts, DNA molecules of Aepyornis eggs were successfully extracted by a group of international researchers and the results were published in 2010 in the Proceedings of the Royal Society B.

facts.statement: Archaeological evidence suggests Aepyornis eggs regularly provided meals for entire human families.
facts.quote: A recent archaeological study found fragments of eggshells among the remains of human fires, suggesting that the eggs regularly provided meals for entire families.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Aepyornis extinction was a secondary effect of diseases transferred from domesticated fowl.
facts.quote: It has also been suggested that the extinction was a secondary effect of human impact due to transfer of hyperdiseases from human commensals, such as chickens and guineafowl.

facts.statement: Aepyornis eggs have been found with a circumference of up to one meter.
facts.quote: Se han encontrados huevos de hasta un metro de circunferencia.

facts.statement: A. maximus is commonly known as the "elephant bird," a term possibly originating from Marco Polo's 1298 reference to the mythical roc.
facts.quote: Aepyornis maximus se conoce comúnmente como el "ave elefante", un término que al parecer se originó de la mítica ave roc por Marco Polo en 1298

facts.statement: Aepyornis was the largest bird in the world, reaching 3 meters in height and weighing nearly half a ton, or 400 kilograms.
facts.quote: Aepyornis era el ave más grande del mundo, con 3 m de altura y un peso de cerca de media tonelada, 400 kg.

facts.statement: Fossilized eggs of Aepyornis have been found with a circumference of over 1 meter and a length of up to 34 centimeters.
facts.quote: Se han encontrado restos de adultos de Aepyornis y huevos que, en algunos casos, tienen una circunferencia de más de 1 m y una longitud de hasta 34 cm.

facts.statement: Like the cassowary, ostrich, rhea, emu, and kiwi, Aepyornis was a flightless bird with a sternum lacking a keel.
facts.quote: Al igual que el casuario, avestruz, ñandú, emú y el kiwi, Aepyornis era un ave que no podía volar y su esternón no tenía quilla.

facts.statement: The National Geographic Society in Washington possesses an intact Aepyornis egg specimen containing an embryonic skeleton, which was given to Luis Marden in 1967.
facts.quote: La National Geographic Society de Washington posee un ejemplar de un huevo de Aepyornis que se le dio a Luis Marden en 1967.

facts.statement: BBC presenter David Attenborough owns an almost complete fossilized eggshell of Aepyornis that he assembled from fragments collected during a visit to Madagascar.
facts.quote: El presentador de la BBC David Attenborough posee una cáscara de huevo fosilizado casi completo, que él ensambló a partir de fragmentos que coleccionó en una visita a Madagascar.

facts.statement: Some authors consider that up to four species existed within the genus Aepyornis, including Aepyornis hildebrandti, Aepyornis gracilis, Aepyornis medius, and Aepyornis maximus.
facts.quote: Según algunos autores, se considera la existencia de hasta cuatro especies dentro del género Aepyornis: Aepyornis hildebrandti Aepyornis gracilis Aepyornis medius Aepyornis maximus

facts.statement: However, later studies recognize only one or two species within the genus: Aepyornis maximus and Aepyornis hildebrandti.
facts.quote: Sin embargo, estudios posteriores reconocen una o dos especies: Aepyornis maximus Aepyornis hildebrandti

facts.statement: The genus Aepyornis was named by Geoffroy in 1850.
facts.quote: PBDB name: Aepyornis (genus), Geoffroy 1850

facts.statement: Aepyornis belongs to the family Aepyornithidae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Aepyornithidae

facts.statement: Aepyornis lived from the Late Pleistocene to the Holocene, between 0.129 and 0 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Late Pleistocene to Holocene (0.129 to 0 million years ago)

rejected.statement: The genus included two species, A. hildebrandti and the larger A. maximus, which is possibly the largest bird ever to have lived.
rejected.quote: The genus had two species, the smaller A. hildebrandti and the larger A. maximus, which is possibly the largest bird ever to have lived.
rejected.reason: statement copies the source wording: 'maximus which is possibly the largest bird ever'

rejected.statement: The volume of an Aepyornis egg is approximately 160 times greater than that of a chicken egg.
rejected.quote: El volumen del huevo es de aproximadamente ciento sesenta veces mayor que un huevo de gallina.
